note: Historical backtests with rules fixed before each run. Research only, not a recommendation. Past results do not predict future returns.

strategies.name: Trend filter (10-month average)
strategies.idea: Hold the S&P 500 while it is above its 10-month moving average, step aside into cash when it falls below.
strategies.bar: Return within 1 point a year of the index, with a worst fall no deeper than 75% of the index's.
strategies.finding: It earned slightly less than the index each year, but its worst fall was less than half as deep (−23% against −51%). It passed as a way to soften crashes, not as a way to earn more.
strategies.caveats: No trading costs or taxes modelled; one market; a pass unlocks only a paper trial, never real money.

strategies.name: Spin-offs
strategies.idea: Buy companies a week after they are split off from a parent, when index funds and parent shareholders often sell them regardless of price. Hold for a year.
strategies.bar: Beat the matching sector fund by at least 10 points on average, across at least 8 cases.

extra.label: Lead without the single best case

strategies.finding: On paper it cleared the bar (+10.3 points), but remove the single best spin-off and the lead drops to +0.1. Five of the thirteen lost to their sector. One lucky pick carried the result.
strategies.caveats: Very small sample; price only, dividends excluded.

strategies.name: Sector momentum
strategies.idea: Each month, hold the sectors that rose most over the past year (skipping the latest month).
strategies.bar: Beat the S&P 500 by at least 2 points a year and win in at least 55% of rolling 3-year windows.
strategies.finding: It did beat the index, by about 1.1 points a year, and fell less in the worst crash. But the lead was well short of the 2 points set in advance, and it won only about half the time. Trading costs, not modelled here, would eat much of the gap.
strategies.caveats: No costs or spreads modelled; the effect has been public since 1993 and may have faded.

strategies.name: Quality companies
strategies.idea: Hold funds of profitable, low-debt companies with lasting advantages, expecting them to beat the market and hold up better in crises.
strategies.bar: Beat a plain S&P 500 fund over 10 years.
strategies.finding: Quality funds trailed the index by about 56 points over ten years, and fell just as far in the 2020 and 2022 sell-offs. The promised protection did not show up.
strategies.caveats: Rules-based funds, so no cherry-picking; about 10–13 years of data; mostly US.

strategies.name: Cheap small companies
strategies.idea: Hold funds of small, cheaply valued companies, a factor that beat the market in long academic histories.
strategies.bar: Beat a plain S&P 500 fund over 20 years, including 2008.
strategies.finding: Over twenty years it returned less than half of what the index did, and fell harder in 2008 and 2020. The long-run academic premium did not appear in this window.
strategies.caveats: US funds only; the premium has been weak since about 2010; regimes can rotate.

strategies.name: Beaten-down sectors
strategies.idea: Buy any sector that fell more than 10% over the past year and hold it for a year, expecting a rebound.
strategies.bar: Average at least 3 points ahead of the S&P 500, with a median at or above zero and a win rate of 50% or more.
strategies.finding: Across 286 cases, buying the fallen sectors trailed the index slightly (−0.6 points on average) and won less than half the time. Cheap stayed cheap about as often as it bounced.
strategies.caveats: Sector timing only, not individual stocks; overlapping windows make the sample look larger than it is.

strategies.name: Holding companies at a discount
strategies.idea: Buy listed investment holding companies that trade below the value of what they own, expecting the gap to close.
strategies.bar: A basket of six European holding companies must beat a world index fund over 5 years.
strategies.finding: The basket returned about a third of the world index. A discount on its own was not an edge: it can stay wide for years.
strategies.caveats: Small, hand-picked basket; currency effects not normalised.

strategies.name: Capital cycle
strategies.idea: Favour industries where years of under-investment have left supply short, and avoid ones where new capacity floods in quickly.
strategies.bar: Industries with slow-to-build supply must beat fast ones by at least 15 points, and beat a simple average of all cases by 10, over 2 and 3 years.
strategies.period: 7 episodes tested after the rules were set

extra.label: Against the simple average of all cases

strategies.finding: The industries the rule favoured did worse, not better, than the ones it warned against. It stays a checklist for thinking, not a ranking to act on.
